title: Forgiving parents
hookLine: forgiving parents, with honesty about what happened

lines: A FATHER'S FAVORITE, A MOTHER'S FAVORITE.
cards: Genesis does not flatter its families. One verse sets up a household's trouble in a single sentence: "And Isaac loved Esau, because he did eat of his venison: but Rebekah loved Jacob." A father with a favorite.
A mother with a different favorite. Two boys growing up under one roof. No gentle editing, no line about how they did their best.
The text just says it. That honesty is a good place to start a hard subject. Today: forgiving parents.

teach.h: ISAAC LOVED ESAU, REBEKAH LOVED JACOB.
teach.b: First, honesty about what happened. Forgiving a parent doesn't begin with excuses. It begins the way Genesis does, by naming it.
The story that follows, of tricks, a stolen blessing and a brother who has to flee, shows what the favoritism cost. Second, the pattern travels.

Years later Jacob has sons of his own, and Genesis says: "Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours." Israel is Jacob's other name.
The favored son becomes the father who plays favorites. The coat is the same wound, handed down in brighter cloth. Third, today's line.
They were young too. A parent who hurts a child was once a child in someone else's house, learning love the way it was shown there. Jacob learned favoritism as the favorite.
Seeing that doesn't make the hurt smaller.
It makes the person who caused it more human, a link in a chain rather than a monster at the top of one. Fourth, honoring is not approving. The commandment says "Honour thy father and thy mother."
Some Jewish and Christian teachers point out that it asks for honor, not agreement, and not pretending.

And nothing here asks anyone to forgive abuse on a timetable, or to go back somewhere unsafe. Where real harm happened, forgiveness, if it comes, can come slowly and from a distance. Today is for something smaller.

how: Jews and Christians read the commandment to honor father and mother alongside the honest family stories of Genesis, and some teachers in both traditions distinguish honoring parents from approving everything they did.

o: going back to a parent no matter how unsafe it is
naming what a parent did, and seeing them as once a child too
agreeing that what your parents did was right after all

s: Genesis presents its families without faults
it says plainly that Isaac loved Esau and Rebekah loved Jacob, and shows what it cost.
the favored son Jacob grew up to play favorites himself
"Israel loved Joseph more than all his children."
seeing a parent as once young means saying the hurt was okay
it doesn't make the hurt smaller; it makes the person more human.

games.q: you're Jacob, grown up, the son your mother favored. now you have sons of your own. what do you do?
o: love them all the same, having learned your lesson.
favor one son, and give him a special coat.
favor the eldest, as custom expects.
games.why: Genesis says Israel loved Joseph more than all his children and made him a coat of many colours. the pattern traveled.

practice: Bring to mind one parent, or whoever raised you; if that relationship holds deep harm, choose someone else, or simply rest in the breath, which is a full practice too.

Otherwise, name one small thing of theirs that still stings, a phrase, a missed game, a habit, then picture them young, before you, being taught by their own parents. Hold both at once: this happened, and they were young too.

wordCard.voice: Forgiving parents. Naming honestly what happened, and seeing the person who did it as someone who was once a child too. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: they were young too. Naming it and seeing them whole can both be true. Until tomorrow.
